newsitem.title: USA: Ford to shut car line, discontinue four vehicles.
newsitem.headline: Ford to shut car line, discontinue four vehicles.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. said Monday it will shut down its Thunderbird and Cougar car assembly line here as part of a plan to discontinue four vehicles at the end of the 1997 model year.
The shutdown, scheduled for the third quarter, will cause Ford to indefinitely idle about 2,500 employees, including 1,800 at the Lorain plant and up to 700 at Ford components plants elsewhere.
In addition to killing off the current Thunderbird and Cougar mid-size coupes, Ford said it will discontinue the Probe sport coupe and the Aerostar minivan this summer.

But Ford said the Thunderbird will be resurrected as a new speciality sports coupe "designed to draw from its early heritage when it was first introduced in 1954." It will be developed from "soon-to-be-launched, multi-vehicle platform" and built at an undisclosed site.
Production of Ford Econoline full-size vans, on a separate assembly line in the Lorain plant, will continue unaffected.
Aerostar production in St. Louis will end August 22, but Ford said the move will not affect employment there, because it plans to boost output of Explorer sport utility vehicles at the same plant.

Production of the Probe will end June 17 at the Auto Alliance International plant in Flat Rock, Mich., but employees at the Ford/Mazda Motor Corp. joint venture will begin building 1998 Mazda models in September. Auto Alliance also will build another Ford product in the future, but Ford officials declined to elaborate on it.

Ford Automotive Operations President Jacques Nasser characterised the decision to drop the vehicles as necessary if the U.S. No. 2 automaker wants to keep up with the shift away from cars. More than 55 percent of Ford's U.S. production is now in the light truck segment, which includes pickup trucks, minivans and sport utility vehicles, he said.
"I think on balance I'm reasonably confident we've got the mix right now. The marketplace will let us know," he said.
The move will most likely result in a second quarter charge of about $150 million, Nasser said.
The charge would not include any ongoing costs, which are still being determined, Nasser said during a conference call with reporters.
